name: For Parents: What a Tool Should Never Collect
title: For Parents: What a Tool Should Never Collect
answer: This idea is a short set of questions parents can put to a school about any AI tool their young child uses: what it collects, how long it keeps it, whether it records voice or face, and whether the child's information is used to improve the company's products. It matters because a tool for preschool through second grade needs very little to do its job, so anything beyond a first name, a class code and a record of completed activities deserves a reason. The book treats careful questions from families as one of the strongest protections available to young children.

sections.body: The idea is that families of the youngest students should be able to ask pointed questions about any AI tool their child meets at school, and that schools should be able to answer them. The problem it solves is quiet over-collection, where a tool is adopted for a simple classroom purpose while its data fields reach much further than that purpose requires. A good early childhood tool collects very little, perhaps a first name or a class code and a record of the activities a child completed. It should not need a photograph of a face, a stored voice recording, a home address, or details about the family's background. Figure 5.7 in the book lists the items that no early childhood tool should collect, which gives parents and staff a concrete reference point instead of a vague worry.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool through second grade, the practice is a conversation rather than a form. A parent asks what the tool collects about their child and how long it is kept, whether voice or face is recorded, and whether the child's information is used to improve the company's products. A teacher or leader answers from what the tool actually does, and the answer should be short, because a good early childhood tool needs only a first name or class code and a record of completed activities. If a tool collects something on the list in Figure 5.7, the parent can ask the school why. Most schools welcome the question, and some discover they had not noticed the field at all.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book offers no research evidence for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than study. What it does report is an incident: the Portland board member described in Chapter 3 found data fields such as place of birth and migrant status in a contract for a reading tool (Willamette Week, 2026). That finding is the book's illustration of how far a contract can drift from a classroom purpose, and it is cited as a news report rather than a trial or a measurement. Figure 5.7 supplies the book's own list of items no early childhood tool should collect, which works as a checklist rather than a research result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the list itself: no photograph of a child's face, no stored voice recording, no home address, and no details about the family's background should be needed by an early childhood tool. The risk the book names is that schools sign contracts without noticing what fields those contracts contain, which is exactly what the Portland board member found. The decisions stay with people, since a parent decides whether to ask and the school decides how to answer and what to do about a field that should not be there. The tool does not police itself, and the book places the protective weight on careful questions from families rather than on the software.
